title: Reaction sensitivity and flux: which reactions matter?
summary: A sorted bar chart of normalised sensitivity coefficients next to a Sankey diagram of normalised flux. Sensitivity shows which rate constants control an output, flux shows where the mass actually goes.

media.alt: Horizontal bar chart of eight normalised reaction sensitivities sorted by magnitude beside a three-stage Sankey diagram of fuel flux.
media.caption: Reference render with synthetic demonstration data (design-system gallery).

source.note: Plot class from the design system's plot taxonomy; synthetic demonstration data.

read_the_figure.question: Which reactions matter?
read_the_figure.axes: Left: horizontal bars, reactions R1 to R8 on y (sorted by absolute value), normalised sensitivity S / max|S| on x from -1 to 1. Right: Sankey from fuel to intermediates to products, band width equal to flux relative to fuel consumption (= 1).
look_at: Which bar is longest? The sign tells promote or inhibit.
Does the sort order follow absolute value, not sign?
In the Sankey, do the widths leaving a node add up to the width entering it?
Which intermediate carries more flux, and how does that tally with the bar chart?
read_the_figure.proves: A few reactions control the output: the short list is where parameter uncertainty must be reduced. The Sankey shows the dominant route. Together they say which steps to measure and which to simplify.
if_wrong: Un-normalised bars: sensitivity units differ between outputs and cannot be compared.
Bars sorted by name or by signed value: the ranking is hidden.
Sankey widths that do not conserve flux: the diagram is a sketch, not data.

terms.meaning: Relative change of an output (delay, speed, peak) per relative change of a rate constant: d ln output / d ln k.
S divided by its largest magnitude so that the longest bar has length 1.
Net rate at which a reaction converts material, often in moles per volume and time, normalised to the fuel consumption.
Flow diagram with band width proportional to flow; flows in equal flows out.

remember: Sensitivity is local: derivative at one operating point.
Sign: positive speeds the output up (here promotes), negative slows it down.
Sort by |S| so the important reactions are on top.
Flux at a node is conserved: width in = width out.

understand.title: Marks and encodings
understand.text: Left: bar length encodes normalised sensitivity, bar side and colour (teal right, rose left) encode the sign, and position on y the rank. Right: nodes are rectangles stacked per stage, band width is the flux, colour keeps the route identity. The Sankey is a flow chart, not a graph with axes.

understand.title: Why this form answers the question
understand.text: Two different questions need two different forms. Which reactions matter is a ranking problem: bars sorted by magnitude on a common baseline are the easiest thing for the eye to compare. Where does the material go is a conservation problem: widths that split and join show it without arithmetic. Putting both side by side gives the explanation (flux) next to the control (sensitivity).

understand.title: Read this reference render
understand.text: Q1: Which reaction matters most? R1, the longest bar at -1.0 (rose, pointing left), so it inhibits the output. Q2: Which is the strongest promoter? R2 at about +0.82, followed by R3 at about +0.55. Q3: What fraction of the fuel goes through intermediate 1? The band into it is 0.55 of the fuel flux, intermediate 2 takes 0.45 and the two sum to 1. Product 1 gets about 0.8 and product 2 about 0.2, so the flux is conserved across the diagram.

understand.title: The must-check list, explained
understand.text: Normalised and sorted: dividing by max|S| makes the longest bar 1 and lets the reader compare reactions; sorting by absolute value turns a bar chart into a ranked list. Both are required, otherwise the long bars are scattered and the units are arbitrary.

understand.title: How it misleads
understand.text: Sensitivity is local: it can change sign or size elsewhere in (T, p, phi). Normalising to the largest bar hides the absolute effect: all bars may be small. A reaction can carry large flux and have no sensitivity, and a rare reaction can have a large one. Sankey bands that cross are hard to follow, and node order is arbitrary.

understand.title: Alternatives
understand.text: A tornado chart with confidence intervals if the sensitivities are uncertain. A reaction-network graph (F9.8) when the topology matters. A table sorted by |S| when you want the numbers.

understand.title: A variant to create
understand.text: Add the reaction equation next to each bar label and the absolute sensitivity value at the bar end; draw a threshold line at |S| = 0.1.

steps.title: Normalised logarithmic sensitivity
steps.note: A finite-difference estimate: raise k by 10 percent and see the output change.

steps.title: Net production rate and flux conservation
steps.note: The Sankey widths are the q_r; the stoichiometric coefficients nu_jr turn them into species production rates.

worked.title: A sensitivity from a 10 percent perturbation
worked.problem: Raising k of one reaction by 10 percent shortens the ignition delay from 100 microseconds to 91 microseconds. Find S, and the normalised value if the largest |S| in the set is 1.12.
worked.answer: S = -0.99: a 1 percent faster reaction gives a 1 percent shorter delay. Normalised, it is -0.88.

analyze.q: R5 has a small bar but R5 might carry a large flux. How could both be true?
analyze.hint: Sensitivity measures control, flux measures throughput.

checks.q: What does a negative bar mean?
checks.answer: Raising that reaction's rate lowers the output; here it inhibits.

checks.q: Delay changes from 200 to 190 microseconds when k rises by 5 percent. Compute S.
The two intermediate bands in the Sankey add to 1 but the products add to 1.00 while one band crossing looks wider. How do you check conservation on such a plot?
checks.answer: Sum the widths entering and leaving each node; if they differ the diagram is mislabelled.
